title: Sacked Ukraine defence minister calls for wartime presidential election

Topic:Unrest, Conflict and War

Ukraine's former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for wartime elections to be held in Ukraine. (TT News Agency: Fredrik Sandberg via Reuters)

Ukraine's ousted defence minister has called for an election in Ukraine.

While wartime elections are prohibited in Ukraine, it is the first call for a leadership challenge to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russia invaded in 2022.

Mykhailo Fedorov has not confirmed whether he would stand in any election, but says the country faces a "crisis of governance".

Ukraine's ousted Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has called for a wartime election, arguing Ukraine faces a "crisis of governance".

It is the first demand of its kind and would be the first leadership challenge to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Under Ukrainian law, holding elections during wartime is prohibited.

But in Mr Fedorov's video address he said "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia".

"We must find a legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war," he said.

The Ukrainian president's decision to fire his popular, tech-savvy 35-year-old Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week baffled many. Analysts say what happens next could be pivotal to the war.

The 35-year-old was a longtime ally of Mr Zelenskyy's until his unexpected firing from the Defence Ministry in July, just six months after he was appointed.

He was the last remaining member of Mr Zelenskyy's first cabinet in 2019.

Unlike his predecessors, Mr Fedorov publicly laid out a strategy to defeat Russia through attrition and technological superiority.

Shortly after his dismissal, a bitter rift was exposed between Mr Fedorov and the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Protests have been held in Kyiv against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's decision to replace Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Thousands of Ukrainians then took to the streets demanding the sacking of Mr Syrskyi, who Mr Zelenskyy later dismissed bowing to public pressure.

Protests in support of Mr Fedorov have continued for the past month in Ukraine.

While Mr Fedorov did not say whether he would stand in an election, one recent poll has indicated the ex-minister could comfortably beat Mr Zelenskyy in a runoff vote, where the top two presidential candidates went head-to-head.

Protesters demand the reinstatement of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister last month. (Reuters: Thomas Peter)

Mr Fedorov said Ukraine faced a "systemic crisis of governance".

"The old system lives by its own rules too often. It protects itself. It is scared of change," he said in his video address.

There has been mixed reaction to the idea of a wartime election within Ukraine.

A poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology earlier this month showed 57 per cent of Ukrainians believed elections should only take place after the war, given that hundreds of thousands of troops were on the front line.

Lesia Bidochko, a policy fellow at the European Policy Institute in Kyiv, said there was still no realistic way to organise a vote, with millions of Ukrainians also living as refugees overseas, displaced within the country, and serving in the military.

Mr Zelenskyy's office had no immediate comment on Mr Fedorov's address.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi, his predecessor General Oleksandr Syrskyi, and new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara at a meeting last month. (Supplied: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service)

Mr Fedorov's statement came just hours after new Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara, a former top special forces operative, was appointed.

He was not Mr Zelenskyy's primary pick for defence minister and was named as a placeholder only after the protests broke out.

Best known as the mastermind of Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia, Mr Khmara steps into the role as Kyiv struggles to defend against mounting Russian ballistic-missile attacks and grinding advances on the front line.

Mr Khmara's appointment also took place just hours after anti-corruption authorities announced charges against a deputy chief of Mr Zelenskyy's office as part of an alleged $4.2 million money-laundering scheme.

Ukraine's anti-corruption authorities revealed they had uncovered a group, including a deputy head of the presidential office, as part of their investigation into an alleged kickback scheme at the state atomic energy agency.

The anti-graft agencies did not name the official, but Mr Zelenskyy dismissed adviser Iryna Mudra shortly after the probe was announced last November.

She has not yet publicly commented on the matter.
